THE SHOT LAB

Practice with a purpose.

Choose a setup, tap the scoring end to set direction and launch speed for a target, then shoot or fine-tune the controls. Drag a black or yellow biscuit from the side of either court view near the dead line onto the court. The supply replenishes after a valid drop. Each color has a limit of four biscuits, including the queued shooter; its supply grays out when full. Drag stationary biscuits to rearrange them. Drops outside the court or onto another biscuit are cancelled. A court click sets both direction and speed using current slickness and drift for an unobstructed shot; collisions can change its destination. Choose one of the four labeled yellow/black St. Pete and Tampa setup buttons. Starting positions keep the biscuit clear of the sloped outside borders. Aim angles are relative to straight down the court.

Switch colors to shoot from either side at the head. Starting position moves from the inside to outside of that color’s starting area. Each color can use four biscuits, including those collected behind the kitchen; the queued shooter counts toward that limit. Practice mode does not enforce turns or a full match. Drag the queued biscuit within its starting area in the full-court view to change its starting position. Click the black starting side to queue black, or the yellow side to queue yellow. Moving the starting position preserves a selected target and recalculates direction and speed.

What the model does

Six-inch discs on a 39' × 6' playing area with 9' scoring triangles and 18" kitchens. Numbers are shown as learning aids. Discs must fit completely inside a scoring cell without touching its ¾ in border to score. The kitchen separator does not invalidate a −10.

Constant sliding friction slows each disc. Slickness maps to a deceleration of 1.47–0.12 ft/s². Optional uniform sideways acceleration approximates drift. Collisions use equal masses and a restitution coefficient of 0.94. These are illustrative parameters, not measurements from the books or a calibrated court.

Biscuits may overhang the court edges and remain in play until completely beyond an edge. The kitchen has angled outside borders. Biscuits fully past an edge are collected behind the far kitchen and still count as used. Short biscuits are also collected when the shot settles. Collected biscuits score zero and do not collide with live biscuits; they can be dragged back onto the court. No cushion rebounds, spin, local surface irregularities, or cue delivery are modeled. Undo and retry preserve the pre-shot setup; retry repeats the previous shot. The queued color switches after a shot settles; Undo restores the previous shooter and settings.

Reading behind the setups

The Clearwater Shuffleboard Club reference library supplies the practice concepts. These notes are original summaries; the books are not reproduced here.

  • Mary Eldridge, Shuffleboard Basics — equipment, scoring, delivery, hammer.
  • Bill Boyes, Ten Strategic Rules — guards, hides, clears and kitchen bait.
  • Floyd Swem, Those Capricious Discs — angles, glancing contacts, combinations and drift.
  • P. C. Bullard, How to Play Shuffleboard — shot selection, blocking and court play.
  • Earl Ball, The Do’s and The Don’ts — clearing, angles and situational play.
  • Bob Zaletel, Keep on Shufflin’ — play on fast Western courts.
  • Bob Zaletel, Mind Over Matter — practice and the mental side of the game; not a physics source.
  • Thom Robertson, Court Evaluation Using Setups, Small Scoring for Doubles, Big Scoring for Doubles, and Making Your Hammer Count — drift testing, scorekeeping and scoring area geometry.

Glen Peltier’s Shuffleboard Strategy is listed for purchase, with no downloadable text on the library page. It was unavailable for review. Source scans contain diagrams and imperfect OCR; this app is a simplified teaching model.
